title: We Can't Offload Teaching to a Ban
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek argues that school bans on student AI use are a retreat from teaching rather than a form of protection. He cites teen survey data showing most students use AI for schoolwork, many worry they are missing out on learning when they do, and few have ever had a teacher explain how it works. Drawing on his years as an English teacher in early 1:1 classrooms, he says schools led with trust and conversation then, and that New York City and Los Angeles Unified are repeating the block-then-reverse cycle now. Blocks also push students to personal devices where no teacher is present, and a Penn study of Turkish math students shows that unguarded AI access helped practice scores but hurt later performance, whereas a hint-giving design did not. He concludes that college will demand thinking without AI and work will demand thinking with it, so discernment must be taught directly, starting with age-appropriate AI literacy and clear communication to parents.
points: Teens say they want discernment about when to use AI and when not to; most report that no teacher has ever explained how it works.
Blocking tools does not stop use: a majority of students who hit a blocked tool simply moved to a personal device where no teacher is in the room.
The Penn experiment suggests the design of the tool and the teaching around it, not access alone, determines whether AI use erodes learning.
Marcinek concedes caution for the youngest students but argues the right response there is a runway of AI literacy, not silence.
Colleges are returning to blue books and proctoring while employers advertise higher pay for AI skills, so students need both unaided thinking and AI fluency.
quotes: They tell me they want to know how to use it better. They want to understand discernment when they use it, and they want to know when not to use it.
In most cases, when a new technology comes along, we react and retreat to a ban or a block. We cloak it in looking out for our kids and trying to protect them.
I put my trust in them before I became a skeptic of their work. If they were going to cheat or circumvent the learning, that was their choice, and ultimately that choice would catch up with them.
But at those grades we should be building a better runway of learning opportunities about AI, what it is and what it is not.
Students who practiced with a standard ChatGPT-style tool did 48 percent better on the practice problems, then scored 17 percent worse than classmates who never had it once the tool was taken away.
College is going to ask our students to think without AI, and work is going to ask them to think with it. Both take the discernment students keep asking me for, and a ban teaches neither.
We need to trust our students and lean into the hard conversations around disruptive technology. We cannot offload the job of educating students to bans that pretend to protect them.
